title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
An AI system was used to create a deepfake interview featuring real public figures, Alan Kohler and Michele Bullock, discussing a fake cryptocurrency platform. The fabricated article was designed to look like legitimate financial news and was deployed as part of a scam to solicit investment in an unlicensed trading system. The failure was at the point of content creation: an AI tool was used to impersonate identifiable people and fabricate their statements without their consent or knowledge.

This represents a deployment of generative AI outside the conditions it should operate in, used intentionally to deceive. The system did not need to assert something false as fact, because deepfake creation is itself the deception. What would have caught it is human verification that the interview actually occurred and that the speakers consented to its use, before the article was distributed.

The regulatory response shows this is part of a broader pattern. ASIC reports that AI-generated impersonation scams are increasing in sophistication and prevalence, with scammers using AI to create fake news articles, reviews, and advertisements as part of coordinated fraud schemes. It is not established whether the deepfake was created with a purpose-built impersonation tool or with a general-purpose AI system used outside its intended use case.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fabricated article featuring ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock discussing a fake cryptocurrency platform called Boulder Sparhaven exemplifies a growing scam trend. The fake interview, which never occurred, depicted Bullock storming out over Kohler's questions about an unlicensed trading system. Australian financial regulator ASIC reports that AI-generated deepfake scams featuring celebrities and politicians are becoming increasingly prevalent and sophisticated, making them harder to detect.

ASIC removed 19,400 scams last year, representing a 182 percent increase, with notable jumps in phishing attempts and fake investment platforms. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, businessman Dick Smith, and billionaire Gina Rinehart are among the most commonly impersonated figures. Scammers create elaborate webs of deception using fake news articles, reviews, websites, and advertisements, then follow up with phone calls and small trust-building payments. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing, while finance presenter Kohler argues that platforms hosting such content should face heavy penalties.
